metric_rationale: The experimental design consists exclusively of compensatory trials where the single most valid discriminating cue favors one option, but the sum of the remaining valid cues favors the other. Take The Best (TTB) will consistently pick the option favored by the first discriminating cue, whereas Weighted Additive (WADD) will typically integrate all cues and pick the opposite option. This metric calculates the proportion of choices that are consistent with TTB's lexicographic rule. TTB will score highly on this metric, while WADD will score very low, creating a massive and highly stable contrast between the two theories.

This metric isolates 'compensatory' trials where the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic and the Weighted Additive (WADD) rule make opposing predictions. Specifically, it identifies trials where the option favored by the single most valid discriminating cue (the TTB winner) has a smaller total number of positive features than the other option. On these trials, TTB will choose the option with the best cue, whereas WADD will tend to choose the option with more overall positive features (since the sum of the lower validities outweighs the single highest validity). The metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the TTB prediction on these specific trials, yielding a value close to 1 for TTB and close to 0 for WADD.

This metric calculates the proportion of times subjects choose the option with more positive features but lower overall validity (ratings [0, 0, 1, 1, 1] vs [1, 1, 0, 0, 0]). Tallying (Equal Weights) will strongly prefer the 3-feature option, resulting in a metric close to 1.0. WADD (Weighted Additive) will prioritize the high-validity features of the 2-feature option, resulting in a metric significantly lower than 0.5.

This metric calculates the proportion of times a subject chooses the option with fewer but more valid features (1, 1, 0, 0, 0) over the option with more but less valid features (0, 0, 1, 1, 1). According to the Weighted Additive (WADD) theory, subjects will prefer the first option because its weighted sum (1.80) is higher than the second's (1.65). Conversely, according to the Tallying (Equal Weights) theory, subjects will strongly prefer the second option because it has more positive features (3 vs 2). This creates a stark contrast: WADD yields a choice proportion > 0.5, whereas Tallying yields a choice proportion < 0.5, reliably discriminating the two theories.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Take-The-Best (TTB) heuristic specifically on trials where the Tallying heuristic is indifferent (i.e., both options have the same total number of positive features). Under the pure Tallying theory, subjects should guess randomly on these trials, yielding a metric value around 0.5. Under the Mixture of Heuristics theory, the TTB component will systematically drive choices toward the option with the highest-validity feature, resulting in a metric value significantly greater than 0.5.

In the experimental design, there are specific 'indifference' trials where both options have the exact same number of positive features (sum_a == sum_b). On these trials, the pure Tallying model is completely indifferent and will choose Option A roughly 50% of the time. However, the Mixture model incorporates a Take-The-Best (TTB) component. The design is structured such that on all indifference trials, Option A possesses the highest-validity discriminating cue. Therefore, the Mixture model will systematically choose Option A more than 50% of the time. By measuring the proportion of Option A choices on these specific trials, we can cleanly separate the two theories.

This metric isolates 'indifference' trials where both options have the exact same number of positive features (equal tally). On these trials, the pure Tallying model predicts a strict 50/50 choice because the total sum of features is tied. The Mixture of Heuristics model, however, will lean towards the option favored by the Take-The-Best (TTB) heuristic (i.e., the option with the highest-validity discriminating cue). By calculating the proportion of choices that align with the TTB prediction on equal-tally trials, we expect a value around 0.5 for Tallying and a value significantly greater than 0.5 for the Mixture model.

By isolating trials where the total number of positive features is equal between Option A and Option B, we perfectly control for the Tallying heuristic, which predicts exactly a 50/50 choice probability (indifference). However, the experimental design ensures that on these specific trials, Option A possesses the highest-validity discriminating cue. Therefore, the Take-The-Best heuristic strongly predicts choosing Option A. The pure Tallying model will yield a metric value around 0.5, whereas the Mixture of Heuristics model (which incorporates Take-The-Best) will significantly deviate above 0.5.

To overcome the high between-subject variance caused by uniformly sampled parameters (beta and epsilon), this metric computes a within-subject Welch's t-statistic for the difference in choice probabilities. We compare Trial 1 (where Option B has unique features) against the pooled Deterministic trials (T2, T4, T5, T6, where Option B has no unique features). Tallying predicts identical choice probabilities for both groups because Option A always has exactly 1 more total positive feature than Option B; therefore, the t-statistic for Tallying will follow a standard normal distribution (mean ~0, variance ~1). Cancellation and Focus predicts a higher probability of choosing B in Trial 1 than in the Deterministic trials, yielding a strongly positive t-statistic. By standardizing the difference by its standard error within each subject, we heavily stabilize the variance for the null theory (Tallying) while amplifying the signal for Cancellation.

This metric calculates the difference in the probability of choosing Option A between Trial 1 and Trial 2. In both trials, Option A has exactly 1 more positive feature than Option B. According to Tallying, the choice probability depends only on the difference in the total sum of positive features. Therefore, Tallying predicts identical choice probabilities for Option A in both trials, meaning the metric should be close to 0. In contrast, Cancellation and Focus eliminates shared features. In Trial 1, after cancellation, Option A has 1 unique positive feature and Option B has 0, leading to a near-deterministic choice for A. In Trial 2, Option A has 2 unique features and Option B has 1, leading to a softer preference (ratio rule). Thus, Cancellation and Focus predicts a significantly higher probability of choosing A in Trial 1 compared to Trial 2, yielding a positive metric.
